title: Time gained
hook: how much time you gain by not watching what your neighbor says or does (Meditations 4.18)

segments.voice: Yesterday: not ten thousand years. Your line was be good while I can. Which good thing did you stop saving for later? Day five hundred fifty-five.

Your phone can tell you how many hours you spent on it last week. It can't tell you how many of those minutes were spent on other people's lives: what a cousin bought, where a classmate went on vacation, what someone said about someone else, and whether your own life measures up. Add them up honestly and it might be the biggest line item in the week. Marcus Aurelius never saw a feed. But he knew the habit, and he did the accounting. Today: time gained.
screen: `HOURS ON YOUR PHONE.` → `HOW MANY ON OTHER PEOPLE'S LIVES?` → `TIME GAINED.`

segments.voice: First, the sum. How much leisure he gains, Marcus writes in the eighteenth entry of book four, who doesn't look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only at what he himself is doing, so that it may be just and holy. The Greek word behind leisure there is close to schole, the free time the Greeks prized, and the root of our word school. Watching others spends it. Second, not their business, yours. Marcus isn't saying ignore people or stop caring. He's saying stop monitoring. Monitoring means checking what others are up to so you can compare, judge or feel better or worse. It costs time, and it buys almost nothing you can use. Third, look at your own work. The attention you take back goes to one question: is what I'm doing just? A carpenter looking at the next bench all day doesn't build a better chair. Fourth, run straight. Marcus finishes with an image from the racetrack. Don't look around at the dark character of others, he says, but run straight along the line, without swerving. Runners who look over their shoulder lose a step every time. Here's what makes this hopeful. You don't need more hours in the day. Many of us already have the time we wish we had. It's just leaking out sideways, into other people's kitchens and arguments and vacations. Close that leak, even partly, and the time comes back on its own.
screen: `HOW MUCH LEISURE HE GAINS.` · `STOP MONITORING.` · `IS WHAT I'M DOING JUST?` · `RUN STRAIGHT ALONG THE LINE.` · then, large: `TIME GAINED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of the place where you most often watch other people: a feed, a group chat, a coworker's desk, a neighbor's driveway. Picture yourself reaching for it today, the way you usually do. Now picture pausing, and turning your attention back to your own next task instead. Feel the minutes you just kept. Decide on one time today when you'll skip that look. The bell holds the time.
Time gained. Marcus says how much leisure you gain by not watching what your neighbor says, does or thinks, and only seeing that your own acts are just. Today's word.
Your line: time gained. Skip one comparison scroll today, and spend those minutes on something of your own. Day five hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes practice Meditations 4.18 by skipping one habit of checking on others, such as a feed, and spending the time on their own work.

myth: Marcus says stop caring about other people
he says stop monitoring them; caring is another thing.
Marcus uses a runner's image in this entry
run straight along the line, without swerving.
the Greek word for leisure is the root of 'school'
schole meant free time, which the Greeks spent on study and talk.

fork.setup: you open an app and see that a friend just got the promotion you wanted. you feel the pull to scroll their whole page. what fits 4.18?
options: scroll it all, to see how they did it.
close it, and turn back to your own next task.
post something to look just as good.
fork.reveal: Marcus says look only at what you yourself are doing, that it be just: the time you don't spend watching is time gained.

original.note: Greek, 'leisure, free time': the root of our word school, and the time Marcus says watching others wastes.

trapdoor: what you thought: mind your own business.
what it means: every minute spent monitoring others is taken from your own work of being just.
what a scholar hears: Marcus's word is euscholia, 'good leisure', from schole, the free time Greek and Roman thinkers prized for study.

notes: 4.18 paraphrased: how much leisure (trouble avoided, in some translations) he gains who does not look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only to what he does himself, that it may be just and pure (holy); do not look around at the depraved morals of others, but run straight along the line without deviating. Long renders the opening as 'how much trouble he avoids'; confirm the Greek is euscholia ('good leisure').
Etymology: English 'school' from Greek schole via Latin schola. Standard; confirm.
